description: Led by Mihaela Vengher (physics student at The Open University, dental technician, Italian Red Cross volunteer), our team includes Stefano Pucci (aerospace engineering graduate, Red Cross), Matteo Casavecchia (environmental chemistry graduate, Red Cross), Andrea Caporicci (Red Cross rescue driver, business planning) and Laura Banaseanu (sports science student,fitness trainer, nutritionist). We love science, art, sport and space, and welcome curious people who like challenges.
summary:
V.I.T.A.L.S. is an intelligent, inclusive and resource-aware health monitoring and decision-support platform developed to protect astronauts during long-duration space missions.
The system integrates personalized medical profiles, physiological and psycho-neurological monitoring, environmental and radiation assessment, interactive 3D visualization, intelligent alerts and predictive simulations.
Unlike conventional monitoring systems, V.I.T.A.L.S. adapts health assessments to each astronaut's medical history, individual characteristics and mission conditions, promoting a more inclusive approach to space exploration.
Scientific datasets from NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) and data and resources provided are integrated directly into computational models and Monte Carlo simulations, connecting real space research with personalized risk assessment.

The platform also proposes human-supervised emergency interventions and a modular architecture designed to minimize unnecessary energy consumption, data transmission and resource use.
By combining scientific evidence, predictive analysis and human-centered decision-making, V.I.T.A.L.S. addresses the challenge of maintaining astronaut health when medical assistance and resources are limited.
Beyond space exploration, its architecture could support healthcare in remote communities, disaster-response operations and other isolated environments on Earth.
details:
V.I.T.A.L.S.

A Personalized, Inclusive and Resource-Aware Astronaut Health Monitoring and Decision Support System

NASA International Space Apps Challenge 2026 — Project Details

Project Overview

V.I.T.A.L.S. is an intelligent, modular and inclusive health monitoring and decision-support system designed to protect astronaut health during long-duration space missions.

The platform combines NASA scientific datasets, personalized clinical information, physiological and environmental monitoring, predictive simulations, intelligent alerts, interactive three-dimensional visualization and human-supervised emergency response within a unified digital environment.

Our goal is to transform health monitoring from a passive process of collecting measurements into an adaptive system that helps astronauts understand their physical and psychological condition, anticipate potential risks and take informed action.

During missions beyond Earth, astronauts may face communication delays, limited medical assistance, restricted energy availability and challenging environmental conditions. V.I.T.A.L.S. is designed to support greater medical autonomy while maintaining human oversight.

The project is built around three fundamental principles: personalized and inclusive healthcare, human-centered decision-making, and responsible management of limited space resources.

1. Personalized Healthcare and True Inclusivity

Every astronaut is different.

A physiological measurement that is normal for one astronaut may require particular attention in another.

Medical history, pre-existing conditions, physical characteristics, physiological baselines, individual vulnerabilities, mission activities and environmental exposure can all influence health risks.

V.I.T.A.L.S. addresses these differences by creating an individualized digital health profile for each astronaut.

The system combines personal medical information with physiological monitoring, environmental conditions and mission parameters to generate individualized assessments.

Instead of relying exclusively on standardized reference values, V.I.T.A.L.S. evaluates health indicators in relation to each astronaut's specific characteristics.

This allows the platform to highlight areas requiring additional attention and support personalized risk assessment.

For example, two astronauts exposed to the same environmental conditions may receive different alerts or risk assessments because of differences in their medical histories or physiological characteristics.

This approach aims to support a more inclusive future for space exploration, in which technological systems are better adapted to different physical abilities, medical needs and individual characteristics.

Our principle is simple: the system should adapt to the astronaut, not the astronaut to the system.

2. NASA Scientific Data Integration

Scientific research and experimental data are fundamental components of V.I.T.A.L.S.

The project incorporates data and scientific resources from NASA, the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), and additional published scientific research.

NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR)

V.I.T.A.L.S. integrates real experimental research data from NASA's Open Science Data Repository directly into computational analyses and selected predictive calculations.

These datasets are not used exclusively as bibliographical references. They contribute to the scientific foundation of the system's analytical and simulation components.

OSDR research supports the investigation of biological responses to spaceflight, including changes associated with altered gravity and other space-related environmental factors.

NASA Human Research Program (HRP)

The project also incorporates scientific information from the following official NASA resources:

  • 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight: scientific information on the principal hazards affecting humans during space exploration.
  • Risks of Human Spaceflight: research on physiological, medical and behavioral risks associated with space missions.
  • Ongoing HRP Research in Space: scientific findings and ongoing investigations into astronaut health and adaptation to space environments.

Canadian Space Agency — Radiation Monitoring

The project references Monitoring Radiation for Astronaut Health, providing scientific and technological information on radiation exposure, monitoring techniques and astronaut protection.

Additional Scientific and Environmental Data

V.I.T.A.L.S. also draws upon additional NASA environmental and biological resources and published studies relevant to spacecraft conditions, planetary environments, radiation, altered gravity and human physiology.

These scientific foundations inform the investigation of:

  • Bone and muscle deterioration in altered gravity.
  • Radiation exposure and associated biological risks.
  • Cardiovascular and physiological changes.
  • Psychological stress, sleep and behavioral health.
  • Environmental hazards and mission-related health risks.

By integrating scientific research into its computational architecture, V.I.T.A.L.S. aims to connect space medicine research with practical health monitoring and decision support.

3. Integrated Physiological, Psychological and Environmental Monitoring

V.I.T.A.L.S. brings different sources of health and mission information together within an interconnected architecture.

Its principal components include:

Personalized Astronaut Profiles

Individual digital profiles containing relevant medical history, baseline physiological parameters and personal information used for health assessment.

Medical Monitoring

Analysis and visualization of physiological indicators, historical measurements, simulated sensor information and potential abnormalities.

Psycho-Neurological Monitoring

A dedicated component focusing on psychological and neurological factors, including stress, sleep, isolation and behavioral well-being.

Environmental Monitoring

Assessment of environmental conditions and potential hazards, including radiation exposure and mission-specific environmental parameters.

Mission Management

An integrated environment connecting crew information, mission conditions, monitoring activities and potential health risks.

Wearable Device Integration

A modular architecture intended to receive and process information from different categories of wearable physiological and environmental monitoring devices.

Interactive 3D Anatomical Visualization

Three-dimensional visualization of the human body allows users to explore anatomical regions and identify areas associated with monitoring alerts.

Visual indicators help astronauts and operators recognize which regions may require additional attention.

Together, these components provide a contextual representation of astronaut health rather than displaying isolated measurements without considering the broader mission environment.

4. Predictive Analysis and Risk Assessment

V.I.T.A.L.S. incorporates computational models and Monte Carlo simulations to investigate potential health changes during space missions.

The analytical approach combines individual baseline information, scientific research, experimental datasets and simulated mission scenarios.

Rather than evaluating only the astronaut's current condition, the system also explores possible future trends and changes in selected health indicators.

This supports the investigation of risks associated with altered gravity, environmental exposure and other mission-related conditions.

By integrating NASA scientific data into selected calculations, the project aims to create a stronger connection between experimental research and individualized health-risk modeling.

The objective is to support preventive monitoring and help users identify conditions requiring closer observation.

Predictive outputs remain experimental decision-support estimates, not clinically validated diagnoses or guaranteed forecasts.

5. Human-Supervised Emergency Response

During long-duration space missions, medical emergencies may occur when immediate assistance from Earth is unavailable.

Communication delays, environmental hazards and logistical limitations can make rapid intervention particularly important.

V.I.T.A.L.S. proposes an emergency-response architecture that combines intelligent alerts, personal medical information, human supervision and potential emergency medical technologies.

When the system identifies a potentially critical condition, it can present an alert accompanied by relevant physiological indicators, individual risk information and environmental context.

A designated human operator at the medical console can assess the situation and determine the appropriate response within established medical protocols.

Human authority remains central to emergency medical decisions.

One proposed hardware extension is an emergency medication delivery device capable of administering an authorized treatment under appropriate medical supervision.

The concept aims to provide a critical intervention window of approximately 20 minutes, potentially allowing time for stabilization, rescue or further medical assistance.

This period represents a design objective rather than a guaranteed therapeutic outcome. The effectiveness and safety of any medication delivery system would require extensive clinical, technical and regulatory validation.

Artificial intelligence is intended to support monitoring, risk assessment and communication, without replacing qualified human medical judgment.

The objective is not to remove humans from medical decision-making, but to provide them with better information when every moment matters.

6. Energy Efficiency, Sustainability and Resource Management

In space, every resource matters.

Long-duration missions operate under significant constraints involving electrical energy, computational capacity, communication bandwidth, equipment, storage and medical supplies.

V.I.T.A.L.S. incorporates resource awareness as a fundamental design objective.

Rather than assuming unlimited processing power, communications or continuously active hardware, the architecture is designed to support more selective and adaptive resource utilization.

Proposed strategies include:

  • Local processing of relevant health information where feasible.
  • Prioritization of critical alerts and essential measurements.
  • Selective sensor activation based on monitoring requirements.
  • Reduced unnecessary data transmission.
  • Offline operation when external communication is unavailable.
  • Modular device integration to accommodate different mission configurations.
  • Prioritization of computational resources according to operational and medical needs.

The objective is to allocate monitoring and computational resources according to the importance of the information being processed.

This approach could reduce unnecessary resource consumption while preserving access to essential health information.

Quantitative energy savings and hardware efficiency remain objectives requiring future measurement and validation.

V.I.T.A.L.S. seeks to combine astronaut safety with responsible technological design, recognizing that sustainability is a practical necessity during space exploration.

7. Modular Hardware and Future Technological Development

V.I.T.A.L.S. is conceived as a modular software platform capable of supporting different hardware configurations and future technological developments.

Proposed extensions include:

Intelligent Wearable Health Devices

Wearable sensors designed to collect physiological measurements and communicate relevant information to the monitoring system.

BioLoad — Intelligent Biomechanical Suit

A proposed wearable technology designed to support personalized musculoskeletal monitoring and explore strategies for maintaining physical function in altered-gravity environments.

Emergency Medication Delivery System

A proposed medical device intended to support rapid, authorized intervention during selected emergency scenarios.

Autonomous Robotic Companion

A multifunctional robotic concept designed to assist with environmental monitoring, inspection, logistical tasks and emergency support.

The robotic companion could potentially interact with the health monitoring architecture, carry small emergency supplies and assist astronauts in demanding or isolated environments.

These hardware concepts form part of the project's broader development vision and are distinct from the demonstrated software prototype.

The modular structure is intended to allow future devices and technologies to be integrated without requiring a complete redesign of the central platform.

8. Development Tools, Programming Languages and Artificial Intelligence

V.I.T.A.L.S. was developed using a combination of programming, scientific research, computational analysis, digital modeling and artificial intelligence-assisted creative tools.

The team used:

  • Python: application development, scientific computing, data processing, analytical algorithms and predictive simulations.
  • ChatGPT: programming assistance, code generation, debugging, technical problem-solving and acceleration of the software development process.
  • Meshy AI: generation and development of three-dimensional models used in the project's visual and technological representations.
  • Gemini AI: assistance with creative development, visual concepts and design exploration.
  • Nano Banana: AI-assisted image generation and visual asset development.
  • Suno AI: creation of original music and audio elements for the project presentation.

Artificial intelligence-assisted tools helped accelerate development and visual production during the hackathon.

The project's scientific objectives, architecture, healthcare concepts, design decisions and functional requirements were established by the team.

The resulting prototype combines computational development with scientific research and multidisciplinary collaboration.

9. Creativity and Multidisciplinary Innovation

The innovation of V.I.T.A.L.S. is not based on a single technology, but on the integration of several complementary approaches within one adaptive system.

Its distinctive features include:

Personalized and Inclusive Health Assessment

Health indicators are interpreted in relation to each astronaut's medical and physiological profile rather than relying exclusively on uniform values.

Scientific Data in Computational Models

NASA experimental datasets contribute directly to selected analytical calculations and predictive simulations.

  • NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR): experimental scientific datasets incorporated into analytical calculations and selected predictive models.
  • NASA and CSA Scientific Resources: scientific foundations for understanding astronaut health risks, radiation exposure, environmental conditions and the effects of spaceflight.

Integrated Human and Environmental Monitoring

Physiological, psychological and environmental factors are considered together to provide a more comprehensive view of astronaut well-being.

Human-Centered Emergency Decision Support

Intelligent monitoring provides contextual information to an operator who retains responsibility for medical intervention decisions.

Resource-Aware Architecture

The system considers the limited availability of energy, communication, computing capacity and medical supplies during space missions.

Modular and Expandable Design

The platform is conceived to accommodate additional sensors, biomechanical devices, emergency-response systems and autonomous robotic technologies.

These elements aim to transform V.I.T.A.L.S. from a conventional monitoring dashboard into an integrated framework for personalized health assessment and decision support.

10. Potential Benefits and Impact Beyond Space

Although V.I.T.A.L.S. was developed for astronaut health monitoring, its underlying concepts could also have applications on Earth.

Many terrestrial environments share challenges with space missions, including geographical isolation, limited medical resources, communication difficulties and restricted access to specialized healthcare.

Potential applications include:

  • Antarctic and polar research stations.
  • Remote scientific expeditions.
  • Disaster-response and humanitarian operations.
  • Isolated rural communities.
  • Remote industrial and research facilities.
  • Other extreme environments where continuous medical support may be unavailable.

A personalized monitoring and decision-support system could help individuals and medical operators recognize potentially significant health changes, manage limited resources and respond more effectively to emergencies.

Its modular architecture could also support adaptation to different populations, operational conditions and available medical technologies.

These terrestrial applications would require appropriate adaptation, testing, clinical validation and compliance with relevant medical regulations.

V.I.T.A.L.S. therefore represents not only a concept for space medicine, but also a potential foundation for more accessible and resilient healthcare systems in challenging environments on Earth.

11. Our Vision — Human-Centered Space Exploration

The future of space exploration will require more than advanced spacecraft and increasingly sophisticated instruments.

It will require technologies capable of understanding individual differences, supporting human judgment, anticipating potential risks and operating responsibly under severe resource constraints.

V.I.T.A.L.S. was designed around the idea that astronauts should not be treated as identical biological systems.

Each individual brings a unique medical history, physical condition, set of capabilities and personal needs.

By combining personalized healthcare, scientific data, predictive computing, intelligent monitoring and responsible resource management, our project aims to contribute to a future in which astronaut healthcare becomes more inclusive, preventive, adaptable and autonomous.

We believe that technological progress should expand human possibilities rather than impose unnecessary limitations on who can participate in exploration.

Our long-term ambition is to help develop systems that protect people not only in space, but wherever distance, isolation and limited resources make healthcare more difficult.

V.I.T.A.L.S. — Because protecting life in space means understanding every individual, anticipating risks and making every resource count.
